title_en: Passion of Irenaeus, Bishop of Sirmium
author: Anonymous (Sirmium)
occasion: To set before the hearers the contest and victory of Irenaeus, bishop of Sirmium, under Diocletian and Maximian. The closing prayer asks Christ to receive Irenaeus and to confirm 'these' (hos), the people of his Catholic church of Sirmium, in the faith.
argument: Irenaeus is arrested and brought before Probus, governor of Pannonia, who orders him to sacrifice to the gods or suffer torture. Irenaeus refuses, citing God's command, welcomes suffering as sharing Christ's passion, and confesses God under torture and imprisonment. When his parents, children, wife, household, neighbours and friends beg him to spare his youth, he answers no one and keeps before his eyes Christ's saying about denying Christ. In a second night hearing he again refuses to sacrifice, says he worships only God and not handmade gods, spiritually disowns wife, children and parents for Christ's sake, is sentenced to drowning, asks for the sword as well, then thanks Christ, prays at the bridge for his spirit and for the Catholic church of Sirmium, is beheaded and thrown into the Sava.

outline.move: Prologue on the Diocletianic persecution introduces Irenaeus, then his first interrogation by Probus ends in torture and his refusal to sacrifice to gods rather than God.

Irenaeus's parents, children, wives, household, neighbours and friends plead with him during torture, but he silently rejects them for Christ's warning about denial, and Probus imprisons him under continuing punishment.

In a midnight second hearing Probus again demands sacrifice, Irenaeus confesses God alone, denies having wife, children or parents except God in light of Christ's command, and Probus sentences him to be thrown into the river.

At Irenaeus's request Probus adds beheading, Irenaeus thanks Christ, prays at the bridge called Basentis for himself and the church of Sirmium, is struck with the sword and thrown into the Sava, with date and doxology.

scripture: The author quotes Scripture in Latin without giving book names: a prohibition of sacrifice to gods other than God echoing Exodus 22:20, Christ's saying on denying Christ before men echoing Matthew 10:33, and Christ's saying on loving father, mother, wife, children and kin above Christ echoing Matthew 10:37. No Psalms occur, so no Psalm numbering is involved. Cite these in modern form as Exod 22:20, Matt 10:33, and Matt 10:37.
uncertain: Date and place of composition are not stated in the text; only the dramatic date under Diocletian and Maximian is given, with martyrdom dated VIII Idy Aprilis.
Whether the surviving Latin is the original language or a translation from Greek is not established from this text alone, despite the catalogue description as a Greek work.
Identity and dates of Probus as governor of Pannonia beyond what the text calls him are not established from the text.
Modern identification of the bridge called Basentis is not established from the text.
Historicity of the family details, dialogue wording, midnight hearing, double sentence of drowning and beheading, and final prayer cannot be established from the text alone.
Text of section 1 iussit eam vexari appears corrupt for eum and its exact original reading is uncertain.

_unresolved_facts.claim: is beheaded and thrown into the Sava
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: iussit eum etiam gladio percuti ... sic itaque percussus gladio a ministris proiectus est in fluvium Savi
_unresolved_facts.fix: is struck with the sword and thrown into the Sava. The source does not say 'beheaded'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: At Irenaeus's request Probus adds beheading
_unresolved_facts.fix: Probus, angered at his boldness, adds death by the sword. The Latin is 'gladio percuti', struck with the sword.

_unresolved_facts.claim: spiritually disowns wife, children and parents for Christ's sake
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Uxorem habes? Irenaeus respondit: Non habeo ... Filii mei deum habent quem et ego, qui potest illos salvare
_unresolved_facts.fix: He answers 'Non habeo' to wife, children and parents, citing Christ's command (Matt 10:37). Later he says 'Filii mei deum habent', which treats the children as his own. Keep both statements literal and add this inconsistency to the uncertain list.
